title: First Code Review
narrative:
You've written your first meaningful feature. It works on your machine. You submit the pull request and wait.

Two hours later, your senior dev comments: "Can you explain why you chose this approach? Also, have you considered edge cases? And can we add a unit test for the happy path?"

Your heart sinks.

choices.text: Defend your architecture confidently

success.text: You explain your reasoning clearly. The senior dev is impressed and approves the PR. "Good thinking!" they write.
success.log: First code review — passed with flying colors!

failure.text: You stammer through your explanation. The PR gets sent back with 12 more comments.

choices.text: Make all the changes silently

success.text: You fix everything they asked for. It's tedious but you learn a lot. PR approved.

failure.text: You fix the obvious ones but miss the deeper issues. Second round of reviews.

choices.text: Ask for a 1:1 walkthrough instead

success.text: Great idea! You both hop on a call. They explain their concerns and you learn tons. PR approved.
success.log: Smart move — learned a lot in 1:1.

failure.text: They're busy and say "just comment on the PR." You're back to square one.

title: 3 AM Production Incident
narrative:
The pager goes off. It's 3:17 AM.

Production database is spiking. Response times are up 500%. Your monitoring dashboard looks like a stock market crash. The CEO just pinged you on Slack: "URGENT - CEO here, we're losing $10k/min!"

You're on call this week. Good luck.

choices.text: Roll back the last deployment

success.text: Quick rollback. The site stabilizes within minutes. The team is relieved. "Nice save!" says your manager.

failure.text: Rollback didn't help — the bug was in the data, not the code. Now you really need to dig in...

choices.text: Dive into logs immediately

success.text: You spot the anomalous query pattern. It's an unoptimized JOIN on a massive table. You fix it and deploy. Solved!
success.log: Found the bug through careful log analysis.

failure.text: You spend 4 hours looking. It turns out to be a DNS issue. The network team had it fixed 2 hours ago.
failure.log: Spent hours debugging. It was DNS.

choices.text: Call a war room meeting

success.text: You rally the team. Everyone pitches in. The senior dev finds the issue within 30 minutes. You learn by osmosis.

failure.text: Everyone's asleep. You get 2 people online and waste an hour trying to coordinate. The senior dev finally joins and fixes it.

choices.text: Restart everything

success.text: Miraculously, restarting the services clears the memory leak. It's a temporary fix but buys time. You're a hero (for now).

failure.text: The restart makes it worse. The database goes down completely. It's been 6 hours and things are still broken.

title: Sprint Planning
narrative:
Sprint planning meeting. The PM presents the backlog: 47 story points of work for a 2-week sprint. The team's velocity is about 30 points.

"Can we fit all of this in?" the PM asks hopefully.

Your team lead looks at you. "What do you think?"

choices.text: Speak up about capacity

success.text: You present data about your team's velocity. The PM understands and prioritizes. Realistic scope set.
success.log: Used data to set realistic expectations.

failure.text: You stammer through your numbers. The PM says "I'll just ask the team to work harder." Everyone groans.

choices.text: Stay silent and take on more work

success.text: You swallow your pride and volunteer for extra tasks. The sprint is stressful but you deliver.
success.log: Took on extra work. Sprint completed.

failure.text: You take on too much. You burn through your first week and have barely made progress. Overtime city.

choices.text: Break down the scope yourself

success.text: You break the 47 points into real tasks after the meeting. Twelve of them are padded. You bring the team a realistic plan. The PM is quiet for a moment, then says, "Okay. That works."
success.log: Broke the scope down into a realistic plan.

failure.text: You spend two days breaking down tasks, but your estimates are wrong — the "simple" integration is a three-week project. The sprint is overcommitted anyway.
failure.log: Your estimates were off. The sprint is still overcommitted.

title: The New Framework Mandate
narrative:
Your company just decided to rewrite everything in a brand new framework that's 3 weeks old. The CTO announced it at all-hands: "This is the future. Everyone needs to learn it by end of quarter."

The framework has 200 GitHub stars and documentation that says "WIP."

Your current project uses the OLD framework.

choices.text: Dive deep — build a prototype over the weekend

success.text: You're a natural. The framework's design philosophy clicks with you. You build an impressive demo that impresses the CTO.
success.log: Learned the new framework over the weekend.

failure.text: The framework is poorly designed. Your prototype breaks. You spend the weekend frustrated and sleep-deprived.
failure.log: Weekend spent fighting a bad framework.

choices.text: Study it methodically during work hours

success.text: You're patient and thorough. By week 3, you're the team's go-to person for framework questions.

failure.text: Work piles up while you study. Your current project slips. You're learning the framework but falling behind.

choices.text: Find the community Discord and ask questions

success.text: You network with other adopters. Someone shares a tutorial that accelerates your learning 10x.

failure.text: The Discord is dead. Only 3 people are active. Nobody can help you.

title: The Requirements Change
narrative:
Product Manager walks in. "Hey, small change — can we make the app work offline, support 12 languages, and add a social feed? We need it by Friday."

You blink. You've been working on a login form.

choices.text: Accept and suffer

success.text: You work weekends. It's painful. But you deliver. Your PM thinks you're a wizard. (They don't know you cried in the bathroom.)

failure.text: You can't deliver. The PM is disappointed. You're now known as "the one who couldn't do it."

choices.text: Push back with data

success.text: You show the PM the effort estimates. They understand and negotiate a realistic timeline. Win-win.
success.log: Successfully pushed back on unrealistic scope.

failure.text: The PM says "just make it happen." You're not taken seriously. The deadline stays.

choices.text: Scream internally

success.text: You channel your rage into focused energy. The requirements actually make sense if you squint. You deliver something reasonable.
success.log: Internal screaming led to unexpected clarity.

failure.text: The requirements are genuinely insane. You deliver something that's 12 languages but doesn't work offline. Compromise fails.

title: The 3 AM Email
narrative:
You're asleep. Your phone buzzes. An email from the CTO at 3:14 AM:

"I know it's late but I had an idea. What if we added AI to everything? Let's discuss tomorrow."

It's not an emergency. It's a "vision."

choices.text: Respond professionally in the morning

success.text: You respond with enthusiasm and schedule a meeting. The CTO's idea is crazy but you channel it into something reasonable.
success.log: Handled the 3 AM email like a pro.

failure.text: You respond too enthusiastically. The CTO thinks you're on board with "AI for everything." You're now tasked with a moonshot project.

choices.text: Don't respond until 9 AM

success.text: You sleep. In the morning, you respond calmly. The CTO's energy has faded. The "vision" becomes a normal discussion.

failure.text: The CTO interprets your silence as agreement. They've already started building a prototype. You're expected to help.

choices.text: Build a quick prototype showing why it won't work

success.text: Before the meeting, you build a 200-line prototype. It fails in exactly the way you predicted. You walk the CTO through it. "Ah," he says, and changes the subject. Working code is a powerful verb.
success.log: Debunked the 3 AM idea with a working prototype.

failure.text: The prototype takes all day and still doesn't quite work. In the meeting the CTO says, "See, it's possible, you just need more resources." The AI project now has a budget.
failure.log: The prototype backfired. The AI project has a budget now.

title: The "Quick" Fix
narrative:
Your senior dev says: "This is a quick fix. Should take 30 minutes."

The "quick fix" involves modifying a file that 47 other files import. The file has no tests. The comment at the top says "DO NOT MODIFY."

The senior dev is on vacation. You're alone.

choices.text: Do it carefully — add tests first

success.text: You add tests, make the change, and verify. It takes 3 hours instead of 30 minutes but nothing breaks.

failure.text: You can't add tests because the code is too tightly coupled. You make the change anyway. It works... for now.
failure.log: Made the change. Prayed nothing broke.

choices.text: Find someone else to do it

success.text: You find a colleague who has capacity. They do it in 30 minutes. You've learned the value of delegation.

failure.text: Everyone is busy. The "quick fix" becomes a "medium fix" becomes a "why didn't we plan for this" fix.

choices.text: Just grind through it and ship

success.text: You read all 47 imports, write the fix, and run the full test suite three times. It holds. You add a comment: "MODIFIED BY [you]. TESTED. DO NOT MODIFY (AGAIN)."
success.log: Shipped the "quick fix" without breaking anything.

failure.text: You ship the fix. It works. Two days later, three services start failing in ways nobody can explain. Your change is in every stack trace.

title: Daily Standup from Hell
narrative:
Daily standup. Your team lead asks: "What did you do yesterday? What will you do today? Any blockers?"

You've been stuck on the same bug for 3 days. Your blocker is... you don't understand the code.

All eyes are on you.

choices.text: Be honest about the blocker

success.text: You admit you need help. A senior dev volunteers to pair with you. You learn a lot in 2 hours.
success.log: Honesty paid off — learned from a senior dev!

failure.text: Your manager sighs. "Figure it out." You go back to staring at the code.
failure.log: Told the truth. Got the axe.

choices.text: Pretend you have a plan

success.text: You bluff your way through. The standup moves on. You have 23 hours to fix the bug.

failure.text: Your manager asks for details. You don't have any. The meeting gets awkward.

choices.text: Fix the blocker overnight before standup

success.text: You stay until 9 PM, stare at the code until it confesses, and find the bug. At standup: "Done. Moving on." Your team lead looks at you like you're a wizard. You are not a wizard. You are tired.

failure.text: You work all night and find... a different bug. The original blocker is still there, and now you have a second one, plus dark circles under your eyes.
failure.log: The all-nighter found a new bug, not the old one.

title: The Merge Conflict
narrative:
You've been working on a feature branch for 2 weeks. Time to merge to main.

There are 47 merge conflicts. Some are in files you don't recognize. One conflict is in a file named "TODO.txt" that contains only the word "help me."

Your coworker who wrote the conflicting code quit last week.

choices.text: Resolve conflicts carefully

success.text: You carefully resolve each conflict. The build passes. You feel like a warrior.

failure.text: You resolve conflicts but break something. The CI pipeline fails. You start over.

choices.text: Delete everything and start fresh

success.text: You nuke the branch and redo the feature. It takes 4 hours but works perfectly.

failure.text: You delete the wrong branch. Your feature is gone. You're starting from zero.

choices.text: Ask a senior dev to help resolve

success.text: A senior dev hops in. They resolve the conflicts in 30 minutes and explain their reasoning. You learn a lot.

failure.text: The senior dev is busy and says 'just resolve them yourself.' You're back to square one.

title: Demo Day Disaster
narrative:
It's demo day. You've been building a feature for 3 weeks. The product team, engineering leads, and CEO are watching.

Your code works on your machine. The staging environment is... questionable.

You hit play. The page loads. Then it crashes.

The CEO raises an eyebrow.

choices.text: Pivot and demo the testing framework instead

success.text: You smoothly pivot: "Actually, let me show you the automated testing that caught 12 bugs." They're impressed.

failure.text: You pivot but the tests are broken too. The demo is a total loss.

choices.text: Own the failure and show the bug tracker

success.text: You say: "The crash is expected — it's in QA. Let me show you what we've fixed." They appreciate the honesty.

failure.text: They don't buy it. The CEO asks why you demoed untested code. You're embarrassed.

choices.text: Stay late, fix the crash, and re-demo

success.text: You stay until the office is empty, find the staging config bug, and re-run the demo for the product team alone. It works. The CEO's assistant sends: "He asked me to say good work." You screenshot it. It's the closest thing to a trophy you own.
success.log: Fixed the demo and re-ran it. Quiet win.

failure.text: You fix the crash, but the re-demo reveals two more bugs. By 2 AM you've learned more about the staging environment than anyone alive, and you're still not done.
failure.log: The re-demo revealed two more bugs.

title: Innovation Day
narrative:
It's company Innovation Day. Everyone is supposed to work on a passion project for 24 hours.

Your manager says: "You can work on anything! Just make sure it adds value to the company."

You have 24 hours. You have an idea. But you've never built anything from scratch before.

Your coworker is building an AI-powered chatbot. Another is building a blockchain-based todo app.

choices.text: Build a small but useful tool

success.text: You build a CLI tool that saves your team 2 hours per week. It's small but everyone loves it.
success.log: Built a useful tool. Team loves it!

failure.text: You build something that doesn't work. The demo is painful.

choices.text: Build something ambitious

success.text: You build a microservice that becomes the foundation for future features. Your manager is impressed.

failure.text: You build something ambitious but unfinished. The demo shows a half-working prototype.

choices.text: Skip the slides — build something that works

success.text: While the chatbot hallucinates and the blockchain todo app runs out of funding, you build a small internal tool that fixes a real annoyance. At the demo, it just... works. Your manager asks if it can be "rolled out to the team." Innovation Day has produced its first actual deliverable.
success.log: Built a small tool that actually works.

failure.text: You spend 24 hours making it work, and it works — but the demo slot went to the blockchain todo app. Your tool gets the last ten minutes, right as the lights dim for dinner.
failure.log: It worked. The demo slot didn't.

title: The Sprint Retrospective
narrative:
Sprint retrospective. Your team missed every deadline this sprint.

The team lead asks: "What went wrong? What can we improve?"

You know the truth: the requirements changed 5 times. The senior dev was out for 2 weeks. The database was down for 3 days.

But if you say that, it sounds like you're making excuses.

choices.text: Give honest but diplomatic feedback

success.text: You share the real issues diplomatically. The team agrees on process improvements. Next sprint is better.

failure.text: Your feedback is taken as complaining. The team lead says "we need more accountability."

choices.text: Say nothing

success.text: You stay quiet. The retro moves on. Nothing changes. You're back to square one next sprint.

failure.text: The team lead calls on you. "What do you think?" You're caught off guard.

choices.text: Quietly fix the top complaint first

success.text: You say little, but by the next sprint the flakiest test in the suite is fixed, the build is half as slow, and nobody can quite explain why the team is in a better mood. The next retro starts with "what changed?"
success.log: Fixed the top complaint before the next retro.

failure.text: You spend the sprint fixing the build, but the team's real complaint was the requirements churn. The build is faster now. The requirements changed six times.

title: The Debugging Marathon
narrative:
You've been staring at this bug for 6 hours. It only happens on Tuesdays. You've tried everything — restarting, reinstalling, even turning your monitor off and on again.

Your teammate walks by and asks what you're working on. You explain the problem. They look at your screen for 30 seconds, point at line 47, and say "You're checking the wrong variable."

It was a typo. A single letter.

choices.text: Do a systematic trace — log every variable at every step

success.text: You methodically trace the execution path. You find the root cause — a race condition in the async handler. It took 2 hours but you understand it completely now.

failure.text: Your logs are too verbose — they flood the console. You can't see the signal through the noise.

choices.text: Take a walk and come back fresh

success.text: You step away for 20 minutes. When you come back, you see the problem immediately. The answer was staring you in the face the whole time.

failure.text: You come back but the bug is still there. You're more frustrated than before.

choices.text: Ask your teammate to pair debug with you

success.text: Your teammate hops in. Together you find the issue in 10 minutes — a missing null check that only triggers under specific conditions.

failure.text: Your teammate is busy and can only spare 5 minutes. They suggest "have you tried turning it off and on again?"

title: The Wrong Algorithm
narrative:
You've been tasked with implementing a search feature. You pick an algorithm you learned in college — it works correctly and the tests pass.

Your senior dev reviews it and says "this is O(n²). On a dataset of 100k items, this will take minutes."

You feel the floor drop out from under you.

choices.text: Implement a binary search — it's O(log n)

success.text: You rewrite the search from scratch. It's faster, cleaner, and the tests still pass. Your senior dev nods approvingly.
success.log: O(log n) is the way to go!

failure.text: Binary search requires sorted input. You forgot that part. The feature is broken in a new way.

choices.text: Ask your senior dev which algorithm to use

success.text: They explain hash maps and you implement a clean O(1) solution. You learn something new.

failure.text: They're in the middle of a crisis and say "figure it out yourself."
failure.log: Left to figure it out alone.

choices.text: Optimize the current implementation — add caching

success.text: You add a simple cache layer. It's not the most elegant solution but it's fast and the tests pass. Your senior dev accepts it for now.

failure.text: The cache introduces stale data bugs. The feature works but returns wrong answers sometimes.

title: The Lucky Bug Fix
narrative:
You're trying to fix a login issue. You change three unrelated lines of code — a variable name, an indentation, and a comment. You don't understand why you made these changes.

You run the tests. They all pass. You deploy. The login issue is fixed.

Your senior dev looks at your changes and says "why did you change the indentation?" You have no idea.

choices.text: Admit you don't know and ask for help

success.text: Your senior dev explains that the indentation was masking a scope issue. You learn about variable scoping and feel smarter.

failure.text: They sigh and say "you shouldn't be deploying code you don't understand."

choices.text: Say "I fixed it, didn't I?" and move on

success.text: Miraculously, your changes were actually correct — the indentation was hiding a bug. Your senior dev is impressed by your "instincts."

failure.text: The login issue comes back 2 days later. Your "fix" was a coincidence. The real bug is still there.

choices.text: Revert everything and start over properly

success.text: You revert, understand the actual problem, and fix it properly. It takes longer but you sleep well at night.

failure.text: You revert but now you've lost track of what you were trying to fix. The login issue is back.

title: The Documentation Gap
narrative:
You need to add a feature to a module that has no documentation. The code is 500 lines long, poorly named, and has no comments.

Your only resource is the existing test file — but even that only covers the happy path.

You're about to make changes to code you don't understand.

choices.text: Read every line of the module carefully

success.text: You spend 3 hours reading. You piece together the logic and understand the data flow. It's not pretty but it's clear enough to add your feature safely.
success.log: Read the code — understood the system.

failure.text: You read every line but the code is intentionally obfuscated. You understand nothing.

choices.text: Add inline comments as you go to understand it

success.text: You annotate the code line by line. By the time you're done, you have a 600-line commented version that explains everything. Your team loves it.

failure.text: You spend so much time commenting that you lose track of the feature. The deadline passes.

choices.text: Write tests first to understand the expected behavior

success.text: You write tests that capture the current behavior. They act as documentation and give you confidence to make changes. Your senior dev says "this is how you do it."

failure.text: The existing behavior is so inconsistent that you can't write reliable tests. You're stuck.

title: The Performance Optimization
narrative:
Your feature works but it's slow. A simple API call that should take 100ms is taking 2 seconds.

Your senior dev says "you're making a database call inside a loop. That's N+1 query problem."

You've never heard of it.

choices.text: Learn about batch queries and fix it properly

success.text: You learn about batch loading and rewrite the query. It goes from 2 seconds to 50ms. You feel like a wizard.

failure.text: You try to batch the queries but the data relationships are complex. You create a new bug.

choices.text: Add caching to speed it up quickly

success.text: You add a simple cache layer. Performance improves dramatically. It's not the most elegant solution but it works.

failure.text: The cache returns stale data. The feature is fast but wrong.

choices.text: Ask your senior dev to show you the right way

success.text: They walk you through it. You learn about N+1 queries, batch loading, and how to use an ORM efficiently.

failure.text: They're busy and say "read the docs."

title: The Unexpected Bug
narrative:
Everything is working perfectly. You've deployed your feature, the tests pass, the product manager is happy.

Then a user reports a bug. It only happens on Safari. And only on MacBooks from 2019. And only when the user has Dark Mode enabled.

You've never seen this bug before. You're not sure how to reproduce it.

choices.text: Set up a browser stack account and test on all devices

success.text: You systematically test across browsers and devices. You reproduce the bug — it's a CSS issue with how Safari handles a specific media query. You fix it.
success.log: Found and fixed the Safari bug!

failure.text: You can't reproduce the bug. You spend hours trying. The user closes the ticket.

choices.text: Ask the user for more details — screenshot, steps, console logs

success.text: The user provides a screenshot and console logs. You see the issue immediately — a JavaScript error that only occurs in Safari. You fix it in 10 minutes.

failure.text: The user is vague. "It doesn't work." You ask for more details. They don't respond.

choices.text: Guess at the fix based on common Safari issues

success.text: You guess that it's a flexbox issue (common in Safari). You add a vendor prefix. It works. The user is happy. You don't know why it worked but it did.

failure.text: Your guess was wrong. The bug is still there. You've wasted time.

title: The Pair Programming Session
narrative:
Your senior dev suggests you pair program on a complex feature. You've never done this before.

You sit (virtually) together and share your screen. They drive, you navigate. Then you switch. It's awkward at first — you're both talking over each other.

After 30 minutes, you start to get into a rhythm.

choices.text: Let them drive and learn from their approach

success.text: You watch how they structure the code, name variables, and handle edge cases. You learn more in 2 hours than you would have in a week alone.

failure.text: You're too passive. You don't ask questions. You don't learn much.

choices.text: Take the wheel and try their approach

success.text: You implement their suggested approach. It's cleaner than your original idea. You feel confident and your code is better.

failure.text: You struggle to implement their approach. You make mistakes and they have to take over.

choices.text: Suggest your own approach and see if they agree

success.text: You propose an alternative. They think about it, then say "actually, that's clever. Let's try it." It works better than their original idea.

failure.text: They politely disagree but don't explain why. You implement their way but you're frustrated.

title: BOSS: The Legacy Monolith
narrative:
Your first BOSS fight. You've been assigned to the "legacy codebase" — a 15-year-old application with no tests, no documentation, and 47 different developers who all touched the same file.

The codebase is written in 3 different languages. The build script requires a specific version of Node that was released in 2014.

Your mission: Add a simple "export to CSV" feature without breaking anything.

The monolith stirs.

choices.text: Brute force it — read the code and hack it in

success.text: You power through the spaghetti code. It's painful but you find a way. The feature works. The monolith groans in submission.

failure.text: You break 3 unrelated features. The monolith fights back. Your manager assigns a senior dev to fix your mess.

choices.text: Write tests first, then refactor incrementally

success.text: You're patient. You write tests, understand the code, and add the feature safely. It takes 3 weeks but it's clean.

failure.text: The code is too tangled to test reliably. Your tests are all flaky. You're stuck.

choices.text: Ask the senior dev who wrote this thing

success.text: The senior dev remembers! They draw a diagram on a whiteboard. Everything clicks. You implement it in 2 days.

failure.text: The senior dev quit 2 years ago. Nobody knows how this works. You're truly on your own.
